newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Liberty focus on Regent St store.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Liberty focus on Regent St store.

text.p: Liberty Plc, the British retailer known for its fine fabrics, which on Friday announced a return to profit after a huge restructuring programme, now plans a major redevelopment of its core Regent Street store.
"Certainly the engine for growth is to build on the success of Regent Street," chairman Denis Cassidy told Reuters.

The redevelopment, which is expected to commence later this year and last three years, will cost in total around 40 million pounds ($65.3 million) and be financed from increased borrowing facilities and the group's strong cash flow position.
"The investment in Regent Street should have a substantial impact on profitability," he said in a telephone interview.
The performance of the Regent Street store in 1996/97 was a "tale of two halves," said group managing director Ian Thomson.

Sales increased two percent in the first half and by eight percent in the second. "It strengthened fairly substantially towards the end of the year and that trend has been continued into the current trading year, hovering just below a double digit increase," Thomson said.

He said the redevelopment plan has two aims. Firstly, it will boost trading space -- by about 50 percent -- for its current merchandise like cosmetics, footwear, household textiles and fashion. Secondly, it will allow new categories of merchandise to be introduced, such as food, beauty services and lingerie.
Asked if Liberty could expand its airport shops -- it has four at London's Heathrow currently -- Thomson said "Gatwick North in the medium term could be an interesting possibility".
He said numerous contacts had been made with airports around the world and he expected "some progress in the coming year".

Earlier, the group reported pretax profit of 4.4 million pounds -- including a exceptional 800,000 pounds profit relating to its major restructuring -- in the year to February 1, after a loss of 16.6 million the year before, when it made an exceptional charge of 18.7 million pounds for the restructuring.

A strategic review led the company to decide to stop making and distributing its distinctive fabrics. As a result, it shut its warehouse in Burnley, northern England and was closing its European textile operations. It also sold its 20 branch shops.
The restructuring is nearly complete. "What remains to be done will be achieved within the original provision," Cassidy said. Ten million pounds of the 18.7 million was used up last year.
Liberty restored its dividend, recommending a final payment of 1.85 pence per share, which equates to a maintained dividend for the year as a whole.

The board seeks a dividend policy more closely related to earnings than in the past, while taking a conservative degree of cover owing to cash needs for redevelopment. It intends to pay an interim dividend of about 30 percent of any intended total. Cassidy said 1996/97's 1.85 pence is "broadly equivalent to about 2.7/2.9 pence for a full year had we paid an interim".

The company's longer term aim is the creation of a premium quality Liberty brand to achieve high quality earnings. During its review it had decided to continue designing its own patterns for fabrics but licence the rights to make and distribute them.

Last year it granted distribution rights to Osborne & Little for its furnishings, fabrics and wallpaper collections. However, it has been unable to agree a licensing arrangement for its Dress Fabrics business, which as a result has been withdrawn from sale for the time being.
Earlier this month, Liberty announced it was selling its 49 percent in Muji, the Japanese retail business to joint venture partner Ryohin Keikaku, part of Saison Group. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
